content: 1. The World Health Organization (WHO) has published an operational handbook on tuberculosis (TB), specifically focusing on the treatment of drug-resistant TB. This document provides detailed guidance on managing such cases and was accessed on March 3, 2022. 2. WHO has also released consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis, with Module 1 dedicated to prevention, including recommendations for TB preventive treatment. This publication was accessed on March 3, 2022. 3. A systematic review and meta-analysis by Khan FA, Minion J, Pai M, et al., published in Clinical Infectious Diseases in 2010, examined the treatment of active tuberculosis in patients co-infected with HIV. The study provided evidence-based insights into managing this dual infection. 4. WHO's consolidated guidelines on HIV prevention, testing, treatment, service delivery, and monitoring, published in 2021, offer a public health approach to managing HIV. These guidelines were accessed on March 3, 2022. 5. The 2010 revision of WHO's recommendations for antiretroviral therapy (ART) for HIV infection in adults and adolescents emphasized a public health approach. This document was accessed on March 3, 2022. 6. WHO's 2016 consolidated guidelines on the use of antiretroviral drugs for treating and preventing HIV infection provide recommendations for a public health approach. This publication was accessed on March 3, 2022. 7. WHO has issued guidelines for managing advanced HIV disease and the rapid initiation of antiretroviral therapy. These guidelines were accessed on March 3, 2022. 8. A study by Chotmongkol V, Jitpimolmard S, and Thavornpitak Y, published in the Journal of the Medical Association of Thailand in 1996, investigated the use of corticosteroids in the treatment of tuberculous meningitis. 9. Kumarvelu S, Prasad K, Khosla A, et al., conducted a randomized controlled trial on the use of dexamethasone in tuberculous meningitis, published in Tubercle and Lung Disease in 1994. 10. Malhotra HS, Garg RK, Singh MK, et al., compared the efficacy of dexamethasone versus intravenous methylprednisolone in patients with tuberculous meningitis in a study published in Annals of Tropical Medicine and Parasitology in 2009. 11. Schoeman JF, Van Zyl LE, Laubscher JA, and Donald PR studied the effects of corticosteroids on intracranial pressure, computed tomography findings, and clinical outcomes in young children with tuberculous meningitis. This research was published in Pediatrics in 1997. 12. Thwaites GE, Nguyen DB, Nguyen HD, et al., evaluated the use of dexamethasone for treating tuberculous meningitis in adolescents and adults in a study published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2004. 13. Mayosi BM, Ntsekhe M, Volmink JA, and Commerford PJ reviewed interventions for treating tuberculous pericarditis in a Cochrane Database systematic review published in 2002. 14. Critchley JA, Young F, Orton L, and Garner P conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis on the use of corticosteroids to prevent mortality in people with tuberculosis, published in The Lancet Infectious Diseases in 2013. 15. Mayosi BM, Ntsekhe M, Bosch J, et al., investigated the use of prednisolone and Mycobacterium indicus pranii in tuberculous pericarditis in a study published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2014. 16. Hakim JG, Ternouth I, Mushangi E, et al., conducted a double-blind randomized placebo-controlled trial on adjunctive prednisolone in the treatment of effusive tuberculous pericarditis in HIV-positive patients, published in Heart in 2000. 17. Reuter H, Burgess LJ, Louw VJ, and Doubell AF shared their experience with adjunctive corticosteroids in managing tuberculous pericarditis in a study published in the Cardiovascular Journal of South Africa in 2006. 18. Schrire V analyzed 160 cases of pericarditis over six years at Groote Schuur Hospital, Cape Town, in a study published in the South African Medical Journal in 1959. 19. Strang JI, Kakaza HH, Gibson DG, et al., conducted a controlled clinical trial on complete open surgical drainage and prednisolone in treating tuberculous pericardial effusion in Transkei, published in The Lancet in 1988. 20. Strang JI, Kakaza HH, Gibson DG, et al., also conducted a controlled trial on prednisolone as an adjunct in treating tuberculous constrictive pericarditis in Transkei, published in The Lancet in 1987. 21. WHO's consolidated guidelines on drug-susceptible tuberculosis treatment recommend a 6-month regimen containing rifampicin (2HRZE/4HR) for new pulmonary TB patients. This strong recommendation is based on high-certainty evidence and remains unchanged from the 2010 guidelines. 22. The 2HRZE/6HE treatment regimen should be phased out, as per WHO's strong recommendation based on high-certainty evidence. 23. Daily dosing throughout the course of therapy is the optimal frequency for new pulmonary TB patients, as strongly recommended by WHO with high-certainty evidence. 24. Fixed-dose combination (FDC) tablets are recommended over separate drug formulations for treating drug-susceptible TB, as per WHO's conditional recommendation based on low-certainty evidence. 25. Sputum smear microscopy may be performed at the end of the intensive phase of treatment for smear-positive pulmonary TB patients treated with first-line drugs, as per WHO's conditional recommendation. 26. If a specimen obtained at the end of the intensive phase (month 2) is smear-positive, sputum smear microscopy should be repeated at the end of month 3, as strongly recommended by WHO. 27. If a specimen obtained at the end of month 3 is smear-positive, sputum culture and drug susceptibility testing (DST) should be performed, as strongly recommended by WHO. 28. Rapid molecular tests are recommended as initial tests for TB and rifampicin resistance in individuals with TB symptoms, regardless of prior TB history. 29. Empirical multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) regimens should be initiated in settings where rapid molecular-based DST results are not routinely available for managing individual patients. 30. National TB control programs should use country-specific drug resistance data to determine MDR-TB levels in patient groups with treatment failure, relapse, or loss to follow-up. 31. For drug-susceptible pulmonary TB patients aged 12 years or older, a 4-month regimen of isoniazid, rifapentine, moxifloxacin, and pyrazinamide may be used as a conditional recommendation. 32. Children and adolescents aged 3 months to 16 years with non-severe TB may receive a 4-month treatment regimen (2HRZ(E)/2HR), as strongly recommended by WHO. 33. ART should be initiated as soon as possible within two weeks of starting TB treatment in people living with HIV, regardless of CD4 cell count. This strong recommendation applies to adults, adolescents, children, and infants.
